guidance.summary: Dafouz and Smit's (2016) ROAD-MAPPING framework analyses English-medium education through six dimensions (roles of English, academic disciplines, language management, agents, practices and processes, internationalisation and glocalisation), offering a tool for learners and teachers to describe their own context. Macaro et al.'s (2018) systematic review found EMI expanding rapidly but evidence on its benefits for language and content learning to be limited, and reported that many content lecturers do not regard language as their responsibility. EAP in EMI and TNE settings should therefore be designed around the local language ecology and actual disciplinary demands rather than imported anglophone-campus models (Jenkins, 2014).

activities.title: Mapping our language ecology
learnerActions: Use simplified ROAD-MAPPING prompts to describe language use on their programme
Compare official language policy with observed practice
Identify where English is essential and where other languages support learning
Discuss what this implies for their English learning priorities
activities.intendedInsight: EMI contexts have their own language ecologies, which determine what academic English is needed.
activities.rationale: ROAD-MAPPING (Dafouz & Smit, 2016) was designed to analyse English-medium education multidimensionally.

activities.title: Lecturer expectations interview
learnerActions: Prepare questions about language expectations for a content lecturer
Interview the lecturer, or analyse a supplied interview
Summarise what the lecturer expects regarding accuracy, terminology and participation
Compare these expectations with the assumptions of their EAP course
activities.intendedInsight: Content lecturers' language expectations may differ from those of EAP courses and are often implicit.
activities.rationale: Macaro et al. (2018) report that EMI lecturers often do not see language support as part of their role, so learners benefit from discovering expectations directly.

difficulties.pattern: 'I must sound like a native speaker to succeed in EMI.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Anxiety about accent and minor errors; reluctance to speak in class.
difficulties.response: Focus on intelligibility and disciplinary precision, and show that interaction among multilingual users of English is the norm in many EMI settings.

difficulties.pattern: Assuming that practices from anglophone campuses apply automatically in an EMI or branch-campus programme, or the reverse.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mismatched expectations about participation, assessment formats or staff roles.
difficulties.response: Investigate local practice through documents, observation and conversations with staff and senior students before generalising.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe how languages are used on an EMI programme they know.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes specific practices (for example lectures in English, discussion in mixed languages, assessment in English) and draws implications for language learning priorities.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes official policy only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Assumes English-only use without evidence.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes in EMI and TNE settings can address this directly. Pre-sessional courses preparing students for EMI should avoid anglophone-campus assumptions. UG and PGT EMI students need discipline-specific support that reflects local practice and the expectations of content lecturers.
reviewNotes: TNE covers diverse models (branch campuses, franchise, validation, joint and dual awards); no TNE-specific source is in the bibliography, so TNE claims are kept general.

guidance.summary: Brown and Levinson's (1987) model, in which the weight of a face-threatening act depends on social distance, relative power and the ranking of the imposition, gives learners a practical heuristic for calibrating mitigation, although its claims to universality and its individualist notion of face have been widely contested. Kasper and Rose (2002) review evidence that pragmatic development often lags behind grammatical development and that instruction combining awareness-raising with practice is beneficial. Economidou-Kogetsidis (2011) shows that staff perceptions of student emails depend on pragmatic choices as well as accuracy, so politeness deserves dedicated attention.

activities.title: Power, distance, imposition ratings
learnerActions: Rate a set of academic scenarios for power, distance and imposition
Predict how much mitigation each needs
Compare predictions with authentic or teacher-written messages for the same scenarios
Revise predictions and note where local norms surprised them
activities.intendedInsight: Mitigation is calibrated to the situation rather than applied uniformly.
activities.rationale: Brown and Levinson's (1987) variables provide a usable heuristic for calibrating politeness, provided they are treated as context-sensitive rather than universal.

activities.title: Noticing mitigation
learnerActions: Read several student-to-staff messages that staff have rated for appropriateness
Highlight mitigation devices, and places where mitigation is absent or excessive
Discuss why some messages were rated as abrupt and others as overly deferential
Rewrite one message at a more appropriate level
activities.intendedInsight: Specific linguistic devices make messages more or less polite, and over-mitigation also has costs.
activities.rationale: Awareness-raising followed by production practice is supported by instructed pragmatics research (Kasper & Rose, 2002); staff ratings follow the perception-based approach of Economidou-Kogetsidis (2011).

difficulties.pattern: Direct forms ('I want…', imperatives) used where English academic settings usually expect mitigation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Bare imperatives or want-statements in emails and requests to staff.
difficulties.response: Explain that many languages mark politeness mainly through honorifics, particles or verb morphology, so a structurally direct English sentence may be a faithful translation of something polite in the L1; then teach English syntactic and lexical mitigation. Do not read directness as rudeness of intent.

difficulties.pattern: Elaborate deference: long compliments, repeated apologies for writing, the purpose buried at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long, highly deferential messages in which the request is hard to find.
difficulties.response: Show that excessive deference can come across as distancing or as obscuring the point; aim for clarity plus proportionate mitigation.

difficulties.pattern: 'Adding please makes anything polite.'
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Please' attached to imperatives or demands ('Please send me the answers today').
difficulties.response: Show that 'please' marks a request but does not reduce the imposition by itself; teach modal, conditional and lexical downgraders and the use of reasons.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to evaluate and rewrite: 'I need the slides from last week. Please send them today.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the absence of mitigation and the imposed deadline, and rewrites with a reason, a modal or conditional request form and no unexplained deadline.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Adds politeness markers but keeps the demand and deadline.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no problem with the original.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: the three variables and core mitigation devices. In-sessional UG and PGT: applying these to real correspondence and meetings. PGR: managing politeness with supervisors, peers, editors and reviewers, where disagreement must often be expressed while maintaining the relationship.
reviewNotes: Critiques of Brown and Levinson's universality claims are not represented in the bibliography; a source could be proposed.

guidance.summary: Requests to staff are among students' most frequent and consequential academic speech acts. Biesenbach-Lucas (2007) found differences between native and non-native speaker students' email requests to faculty in directness and in the use of mitigating modification, and Economidou-Kogetsidis (2011) found that lecturers perceived unmitigated or imposing requests negatively even when they were grammatically accurate. Teach request structure (head act, internal and external modification) using categories from cross-cultural request research (Blum-Kulka et al., 1989), always calibrated to the imposition and to any procedure that governs the request.

activities.title: Imposition ladder
learnerActions: Rank a set of academic requests by imposition, from asking for a link to asking for a reference at short notice
Write requests at three points on the ladder
Compare modification choices with peers and with models
Identify which requests are governed by formal procedures
activities.intendedInsight: Mitigation should increase with imposition, and some requests belong in formal processes rather than personal appeals.
activities.rationale: Request research describes how modification varies with situational factors and how learners may under- or over-modify (Blum-Kulka et al., 1989; Biesenbach-Lucas, 2007).

activities.title: Request anatomy
learnerActions: Analyse student requests into opening, reason, head act, modification and closing
Identify missing or excessive elements
Rewrite one request twice, as an email and as a spoken request in person
Get peer feedback on clarity and tone
activities.intendedInsight: Requests have identifiable parts, each with a function that can be adjusted.
activities.rationale: Analysing request components follows the coding categories widely used in request research (Blum-Kulka et al., 1989) and makes pragmatic choices teachable (Kasper & Rose, 2002).

difficulties.pattern: Requests framed as needs or obligations ('I need an extension', 'You should send me').
difficulties.revealedBy: Want and need statements used as the head act in requests to staff.
difficulties.response: Teach preparatory forms ('Could you…', 'Would it be possible to…') and conditional mitigation. Do not simply ban 'I need'; a need statement with a clear reason can be appropriate. Expect these forms to develop gradually rather than all at once.

difficulties.pattern: Imposing time pressure ('Please reply as soon as possible').
difficulties.revealedBy: Urgency markers without explanation, often carried over from service or business email templates.
difficulties.response: Show how unexplained time demands increase the imposition, and teach how to signal genuine urgency with a reason.

difficulties.pattern: 'It is more polite to give all the background before I ask.'
difficulties.revealedBy: The request appears only in the final lines or is merely implied.
difficulties.response: Teach an early purpose statement followed by context, and show how busy recipients read emails. Acknowledge that context-first ordering is valued in many settings and is not wrong in principle.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a request for a three-day extension because of illness.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Refers to the formal procedure, states the request clearly, gives the reason, mitigates proportionately and offers evidence.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States a clear request with a reason but ignores the procedure, or is clearly under- or over-mitigated.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Makes a demand without a reason or any reference to procedure.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: core request forms and the idea of imposition. In-sessional UG and PGT: real requests for meetings, feedback, extensions and references. PGR: high-imposition requests to supervisors, external researchers, data gatekeepers and editors, often across institutions.
reviewNotes: The summary of Biesenbach-Lucas (2007) is given at a general level (differences in directness and modification); verify detailed claims against the article before adding specifics.

guidance.summary: Email to staff is a hybrid genre between letter and conversation, and student emails are judged on content, structure and politeness together. Biesenbach-Lucas (2007) and Economidou-Kogetsidis (2011) document variation in how students open, frame and close emails and mitigate requests, and Economidou-Kogetsidis shows how such features shape lecturers' perceptions. Teach email as a genre with recognisable moves (subject, greeting, identification, purpose, context, request, closing, signature) whose realisation varies with recipient and local norms, using analysis of authentic examples and rewriting.

activities.title: Inbox triage
learnerActions: Read a set of anonymised or invented student emails as if they were a busy lecturer
Decide which could be answered immediately and why
Identify what made the others hard to answer (missing information, unclear purpose, tone)
Rewrite one so that it could be answered in a single reply
activities.intendedInsight: An email succeeds when it makes the recipient's task easy.
activities.rationale: Taking the recipient's perspective helps learners see how structure and politeness affect perception (Economidou-Kogetsidis, 2011).

activities.title: Move analysis and rewriting
learnerActions: Identify the moves in several model emails
Compare openings and closings across emails to different recipients
Write an email for a given scenario
Peer-review it with a move checklist and revise
activities.intendedInsight: Emails have a predictable structure that varies with recipient and purpose.
activities.rationale: Move analysis makes the genre's structure explicit, and Biesenbach-Lucas (2007) shows variation in how students realise its elements.

difficulties.pattern: Blank or uninformative subject lines ('Hello', 'Question').
difficulties.revealedBy: Emails without a subject or with a generic one, which staff may overlook or deprioritise.
difficulties.response: Practise subject lines that include the module code and purpose, and have learners sort an inbox by subject line alone to see the effect.

difficulties.pattern: Writing as in instant messaging: no greeting, lower case, abbreviations.
difficulties.revealedBy: Messages such as 'hi can u send the slides'.
difficulties.response: Contrast channels and audiences and show how such messages may be perceived by staff. Frame this as audience adaptation, not a moral failing.

difficulties.pattern: No identifying details (full name, module, student number).
difficulties.revealedBy: Staff cannot tell who the sender is or which module the query concerns.
difficulties.response: Provide a signature template and a pre-send checklist.

diagnostic.task: Give a scenario and ten minutes to write the email.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All moves present; informative subject line; clear early purpose; proportionate mitigation; identifying details.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Clear purpose but a weak subject line, missing identification or uneven tone.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Unclear purpose, inappropriate address or an unmitigated demand.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: the core genre and its moves. In-sessional UG and PGT: emails to different roles (administrators, tutors, dissertation supervisors). PGR: emails to prospective supervisors, external academics, conference organisers and editors; correspondence with editors overlaps with pub.cover-letters.

guidance.summary: Office hours and tutorials are an institutional genre with recurring phases (opening, stating purpose, discussion, closing) and a status asymmetry that students must manage. Bardovi-Harlig and Hartford (1990) found differences between native and non-native speaker students in academic advising sessions in how suggestions and rejections were made and in the use of status-preserving mitigation, and Biber (2006) describes office hours as a distinct interactive university register. Preparing specific questions and rehearsing openings, clarification requests and closings builds the confidence to use an often under-used resource.

activities.title: Office hour rehearsal
learnerActions: Prepare for a real or simulated meeting: purpose, two or three questions, materials
Role-play with a peer or teacher playing a tutor who gives brief or vague advice
Practise clarification requests and a closing summary of actions
Debrief on what worked and what to change
activities.intendedInsight: Preparation and specific questions make short meetings productive.
activities.rationale: Rehearsing interactional sequences with feedback supports pragmatic development (Kasper & Rose, 2002).

activities.title: Analysing meeting talk
learnerActions: Listen to a recording or read a transcript of an office hour or tutorial
Identify the phases and who initiates each
Note the language used to frame purpose, ask for clarification and close
Compile a short personal phrase bank
activities.intendedInsight: Meetings follow patterns that can be anticipated and prepared for.
activities.rationale: Biber (2006) documents office hours as a distinctive university register; examining it makes its patterns available to learners.

difficulties.pattern: 'I shouldn't take up the professor's time unless I have a serious problem.'
difficulties.revealedBy: No attendance at office hours; questions saved until after assessment.
difficulties.response: Explain what office hours are for at this institution and give concrete reasons to attend (checking a plan, discussing feedback). Arrange a first visit as a class task where possible.

difficulties.pattern: Arriving without specific questions or materials.
difficulties.revealedBy: Meetings end without clear outcomes; learners report that the meeting 'did not help'.
difficulties.response: Use a short preparation sheet (purpose, questions, materials, desired outcome) before each meeting.

difficulties.pattern: Accepting vague advice without asking what it means.
difficulties.revealedBy: The learner agrees during the meeting but cannot act on the advice afterwards.
difficulties.response: Practise clarification and summarising moves and present them as expected, not as challenges to the tutor.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'You have ten minutes with your tutor about your essay feedback. How will you use the time?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names specific questions about particular comments, brings the draft and feedback, and plans to summarise agreed actions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States a general intention to 'discuss the feedback'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Would not go, or would not know what to ask.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: what office hours are and why to use them. Pre-sessional: rehearsal using the destination institution's arrangements. In-sessional UG and PGT: real feedback tutorials, personal tutor meetings and dissertation meetings. PGR supervision meetings are covered by res.supervision.
reviewNotes: Bardovi-Harlig and Hartford (1990) is a proposed reference; if it is not verified, the summary should rely on biber2006 and kasperrose2002.

guidance.summary: Extenuating circumstances statements, appeals and complaints are institutional genres judged against regulations, and their success depends on procedural fit, relevant evidence and a measured tone more than on persuasion. Bhatia's (1993) analysis of professional and legal genres shows how such texts are shaped by institutional purposes and constraints, and move analysis (Swales, 1990) can help learners identify what their own institution's forms and guidance expect. Because procedures, terminology and grounds differ between institutions, teaching should always work from local regulations and signpost student advice services.

activities.title: Procedure first
learnerActions: Read their institution's extenuating circumstances or appeals policy
Identify the permitted grounds, deadlines, evidence required and possible outcomes
Turn these into a checklist
Apply the checklist to a sample case
activities.intendedInsight: The regulation defines what a statement must do.
activities.rationale: Analysing the institutional constraints on a genre reflects Bhatia's (1993) approach to professional genres.

activities.title: From narrative to statement
learnerActions: Read an emotional, unordered account of events
Select the relevant facts and put them in chronological order with dates
Link each circumstance to its effect on assessment
Rewrite in a measured register and compare versions with peers
activities.intendedInsight: Selecting and ordering facts, rather than intensifying emotion, makes a statement effective.
activities.rationale: Transforming a narrative into an institutional genre makes its moves and register explicit (Swales, 1990). This is a practice-based proposal.

difficulties.pattern: Appealing to effort or deserving ('I worked very hard on this module') rather than to permitted grounds.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements that emphasise effort, past grades or personal need.
difficulties.response: Show the grounds listed in the regulations and explain that effort or need alone is not usually a ground.

difficulties.pattern: An accusatory or emotional tone toward staff.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements that blame named tutors or use emotive language.
difficulties.response: Separate facts from evaluation; suggest drafting, waiting and revising, and using student advice services for support.

difficulties.pattern: Disclosing far more personal or medical detail than the process requires.
difficulties.revealedBy: Lengthy personal narratives, sometimes with sensitive details unrelated to the claim.
difficulties.response: Explain that evidence and confidentiality procedures exist; disclose what is needed to establish the circumstance and its effect.

diagnostic.task: Give a disordered case and ask which details belong in an extenuating circumstances statement and in what order.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Selects relevant, dated, evidenced facts, orders them chronologically, links them to assessment impact and excludes irrelevant detail.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Selects relevant facts but omits the link to impact or the outcome requested.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Includes everything, or focuses on effort and sympathy.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: awareness of the procedures and when to use them, since circumstances can arise during these courses too. In-sessional UG and PGT: drafting when needed, alongside student advice services. Teachers should not advise on live cases beyond language and should refer students to advice services.
reviewNotes: No research on student extenuating circumstances or appeal statements was found in the bibliography; guidance is practice-based.
Terminology (extenuating versus mitigating circumstances) and permitted grounds vary by institution and country.

guidance.summary: Apologies redress a threat to the hearer's face while threatening the speaker's own (Brown & Levinson, 1987). Cross-cultural research identifies recurring apology strategies (an explicit apology expression, an account, acknowledgement of responsibility, an offer of repair and a promise of forbearance) whose selection varies with situation and language (Blum-Kulka et al., 1989), and Kasper and Rose (2002) show these develop with exposure and instruction. In academic contexts an effective apology is usually brief, offers repair and connects to any formal process, such as absence reporting.

activities.title: Apology components
learnerActions: Analyse several apologies to staff for their components
Rate each for appropriateness and explain the ratings
Rewrite weaker examples to add repair and remove over-disclosure
Discuss which situations also need a formal procedure
activities.intendedInsight: Effective apologies include repair, not only regret.
activities.rationale: Component analysis follows the categories of cross-cultural apology research (Blum-Kulka et al., 1989).

activities.title: Spoken apology role-play
learnerActions: Role-play arriving late to a seminar, missing a meeting and missing a group deadline
Practise a brief spoken apology with an account and repair
Give and receive peer feedback
Repeat with a different relationship (peer versus tutor)
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken apologies should be brief and proportionate, and vary with the relationship.
activities.rationale: Practice across varied power and distance conditions builds sociopragmatic flexibility (Kasper & Rose, 2002).

difficulties.pattern: 'The more detail I give, the more sincere I seem.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Long accounts with personal detail and little repair.
difficulties.response: Show that brief accounts are the norm in this context and that detailed evidence belongs in formal processes, not personal apologies.

difficulties.pattern: Giving an explanation but no explicit apology expression.
difficulties.revealedBy: Messages that explain the absence but never say sorry or acknowledge the inconvenience.
difficulties.response: Teach explicit apology expressions alongside accounts and show how their absence may be read. Do not assume the learner intended no apology.

difficulties.pattern: Excessive self-criticism and repeated apologies.
difficulties.revealedBy: Multiple apologies in one message; self-deprecating language.
difficulties.response: Model proportionate apologies and reassure learners that a single, sincere apology with repair is sufficient.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to apologise, in writing or speech, to a tutor for missing a scheduled meeting.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explicit apology, brief relevant account and concrete repair such as rescheduling.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Apology without repair, or with excessive detail.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No apology, or an account that blames the tutor or institution.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: core apology forms in speech and writing. In-sessional UG and PGT: real situations, with explicit links to absence reporting, extensions and extenuating circumstances processes.
reviewNotes: Blum-Kulka et al. (1989) is a proposed reference.

guidance.summary: Asynchronous forums blend features of speech and writing; effective posts combine a clear point, support from readings and explicit engagement with peers. Hyland's (2005) model of stance and engagement provides resources for positioning oneself and addressing readers, and Coffin, Painter and Hewings (2005) analysed patterns of argument in tertiary asynchronous conferencing, indicating that sustained debate does not emerge automatically. Teaching should model replies that build on and challenge others and clarify local expectations for assessed posts.

activities.title: Reply moves
learnerActions: Analyse a forum thread for reply types (agree, extend, question, challenge, synthesise)
Identify which moves advanced the discussion
Write two replies using different moves
Peer-evaluate the replies for engagement and support
activities.intendedInsight: Replies that extend, question or challenge advance discussion more than agreement alone.
activities.rationale: Engagement resources (Hyland, 2005) help writers position themselves in relation to readers and other voices.

activities.title: Post makeover
learnerActions: Read a weak post (off-topic, unsupported or written in text-speak)
Revise it for point, support, engagement and register
Compare revisions in groups
Agree a checklist for future posts
activities.intendedInsight: Forum register sits between conversation and formal academic prose and still rewards support and focus.
activities.rationale: Explicit criteria help learners meet assessed forum expectations; Coffin et al. (2005) suggest that the quality of argument in forums varies and benefits from attention.

difficulties.pattern: Replies that only agree ('Great post, I totally agree').
difficulties.revealedBy: Threads made up of agreement with no development.
difficulties.response: Teach mitigated disagreement and extension moves and show that collegial challenge is expected.

difficulties.pattern: Posting a self-contained mini-essay that ignores other contributions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long posts that never mention peers' points.
difficulties.response: Model dialogic engagement by naming and responding to specific peer points.

difficulties.pattern: Register that is too informal or too formal for the forum.
difficulties.revealedBy: Text-speak at one extreme, essay-style impersonality at the other.
difficulties.response: Show model posts from the learner's own course and discuss what the forum's purpose requires.

diagnostic.task: Give a short thread and ask for a reply of about 150 words.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Engages a specific peer point, adds supported content and handles agreement or disagreement collegially.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Engages peers but without support, or adds support without engaging peers.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Generic agreement or an off-topic post.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: practice on the course VLE as part of blended provision. In-sessional UG and PGT: assessed forums, particularly in online and distance programmes, where posts may carry significant marks.
reviewNotes: Coffin et al. (2005) is a proposed reference; if it is not verified, rely on hyland2005stance alone.

guidance.summary: Students now communicate through several channels (email, VLE messaging and forums, enquiry systems, group chats and collaboration platforms), each with different norms of formality, privacy and response time. Biesenbach-Lucas (2007) treats student–faculty email as a medium whose politeness conventions are less settled than those of traditional letters, and Economidou-Kogetsidis (2011) illustrates how demands for urgent replies can affect lecturers' perceptions. Teach channel choice as a decision about purpose, audience, privacy and urgency, grounded in each department's stated policy.

activities.title: Channel sort
learnerActions: Sort a set of scenarios into the channels available at their institution
Justify each choice with reference to institutional or module guidance
Compare choices with peers and resolve disagreements
Make a personal reference card for future use
activities.intendedInsight: Channel choice is part of the message and is governed by local norms.
activities.rationale: Making channel norms explicit addresses an area where conventions are often unstated and still changing (Biesenbach-Lucas, 2007).

activities.title: Waiting and following up
learnerActions: Find staff response-time statements in module handbooks or staff pages
Discuss what to do while waiting for a reply
Draft a polite follow-up to be sent after a reasonable interval
Compare follow-ups and identify what makes them appropriate
activities.intendedInsight: Response times have limits, and follow-ups need sensible spacing and mitigation.
activities.rationale: Economidou-Kogetsidis (2011) discusses time-pressure demands as a source of negative perceptions in student emails.

difficulties.pattern: Contacting staff through personal social media or messaging apps.
difficulties.revealedBy: Messages to staff on personal accounts, sometimes outside working hours.
difficulties.response: Explain institutional boundaries and the reasons for them, while acknowledging that some staff and institutions do use such channels; check local norms.

difficulties.pattern: Sending several follow-ups within hours.
difficulties.revealedBy: Chains of messages on the same query, often driven by anxiety about deadlines.
difficulties.response: Discuss reasonable response times and alternative sources of help while waiting; draft a single follow-up together.

difficulties.pattern: Sharing private information in group or public channels.
difficulties.revealedBy: Personal circumstances, marks or health details posted in forums or group chats.
difficulties.response: Distinguish public from private channels explicitly and practise deciding what belongs where.

diagnostic.task: Give six short scenarios and ask which channel the learner would use and when they would expect a reply.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Chooses channels in line with stated norms, protects privacy, and sets realistic expectations about replies and follow-ups.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Most choices appropriate, but privacy or response-time expectations misjudged.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses one channel for everything or chooses personal channels for staff contact.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: introducing institutional channels and their purposes. In-sessional UG and PGT: managing group-work channels alongside staff communication. PGR: professional multichannel communication with supervisors, labs, collaborators and external partners.
reviewNotes: Channel norms are changing quickly, and no source in the bibliography addresses multichannel student–staff communication directly.

guidance.summary: Hyland's (2004) analysis of dissertation acknowledgements identified a three-tier structure (reflecting, thanking and announcing moves) and showed the genre's role in self-presentation and academic networking. Article acknowledgements serve additional functions: disclosing funding and recognising contributors who do not meet authorship criteria (ICMJE, 2025; Brand et al., 2015). Teaching should combine move analysis with institutional and journal requirements and attention to confidentiality.

activities.title: Move analysis of acknowledgements
learnerActions: Analyse several thesis or dissertation acknowledgements from their field
Identify the moves and their order
Note variation in register and length
Draft their own acknowledgement
activities.intendedInsight: Acknowledgements follow recognisable conventions while allowing personal expression.
activities.rationale: Hyland (2004) identifies the moves of dissertation acknowledgements, providing a basis for analysis.

activities.title: Who goes where?
learnerActions: Sort a list of contributors into authors, acknowledged contributors and those not acknowledged
Justify decisions using ICMJE criteria or CRediT roles
Draft a funding statement
Compare decisions with peers
activities.intendedInsight: Acknowledgement and authorship are distinct, with ethical implications.
activities.rationale: Authorship criteria (ICMJE, 2025) and contributor role taxonomies (Brand et al., 2015) define who is acknowledged rather than listed as an author.

difficulties.pattern: Naming participants or organisations that were promised anonymity.
difficulties.revealedBy: Acknowledgements that identify research sites or participants by name.
difficulties.response: Check consent and ethics documentation before naming anyone; thank participants collectively where anonymity was promised.

difficulties.pattern: Register that is either extremely effusive or perfunctory.
difficulties.revealedBy: Very long, emotional acknowledgements or a single generic line.
difficulties.response: Show a range of models from the learner's field and institution and discuss audience.

difficulties.pattern: Offering authorship as a form of thanks, or acknowledging someone whose contribution merits authorship.
difficulties.revealedBy: Proposed author lists that include people who only provided resources, or acknowledgements of substantial intellectual contributors.
difficulties.response: Revisit authorship criteria and discuss with supervisors.

diagnostic.task: Give a list of contributors and ask the learner to decide who is acknowledged, who might be an author and how anonymous participants are thanked.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correctly distinguishes authors and acknowledged contributors, includes funding details and protects anonymity.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mostly correct but omits funding or names an anonymous participant.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Confuses authorship and acknowledgement or omits required elements.

guidance.contextNotes: UG and PGT dissertation acknowledgements are usually short and optional. PGR thesis acknowledgements are longer and more personal. Article acknowledgements are formulaic and often include required funding and conflict-of-interest statements.
reviewNotes: Hyland (2004) is a proposed reference; verify before publication.

proposedReferences.apa: Blum-Kulka, S., House, J., & Kasper, G. (Eds.). (1989). *Cross-cultural pragmatics: Requests and apologies*. Ablex.
proposedReferences.note: High confidence: the standard edited volume reporting the Cross-Cultural Speech Act Realization Project (CCSARP). No DOI. Supports the request and apology strategy categories used in prg.requests and prg.apologising-explaining.

proposedReferences.apa: Hyland, K. (2004). Graduates' gratitude: The generic structure of dissertation acknowledgements. *English for Specific Purposes, 23*(3), 303–324.
proposedReferences.note: High confidence in author, year, title and journal. Volume, issue and page range are believed correct but should be checked; DOI omitted because I am not certain of it. Supports the move structure (reflecting, thanking, announcing) cited in prg.acknowledgements.

proposedReferences.note: High confidence in authors, year, title and journal; issue and pages should be verified. DOI omitted. Used for differences in suggestions, rejections and status-preserving strategies in advising sessions (prg.office-hours).

authorNotes: Cross-group cycle risk: acu.disciplinary-knowledge <- crt.evidence-types, acu.transition <- idn.intercultural-communication, acu.critical-eap <- idn.standards-legitimacy and acu.emi-tne <- idn.elf. The CRT and IDN authors should not make those topics depend on ACU topics.

voc.university-terminology and acu.university-structures / acu.teaching-formats develop together. I left ACU topics without VOC prerequisites so that VOC can safely add voc.university-terminology <- acu.university-structures (soft) if it wants to.

Overlap: ges.genre-concept ('Genre and discourse community') duplicates the discourse-community half of acu.discourse-communities. Suggest narrowing ges.genre-concept to genre and adding ges.genre-concept <- acu.discourse-communities.
Overlap: acu.academic-expectations overlaps lrn.independent-study, lrn.autonomy and crt.concept. Suggest those take acu.academic-expectations as a soft prerequisite rather than the reverse.
Overlap: acu.hidden-curriculum overlaps fbk.marking-criteria and fbk.feedback-literacy, which concern tacit criteria too. Suggest the FBK topics take acu.hidden-curriculum as a soft prerequisite.

Scope: acu.academic-literacies and acu.critical-eap are mainly teacher and curriculum perspectives. Their learner-facing scope is narrowed to PGT/PGR or to interpreting one's own experience. Consider flagging them as 'practitioner knowledge' in the build.
Gap: no topic covers student voice and representation (module evaluation, course reps, student-staff committees), which is how learners can legitimately act on acu.critical-eap. Consider adding one.

Overlap: fbk.seeking-feedback (SOCIOPRAGMATIC) overlaps prg.requests and prg.office-hours. Suggest fbk.seeking-feedback take prg.requests as a prerequisite and not the reverse. I made no PRG topic depend on FBK.

Overlap: prg.messaging-channels overlaps dig.digital-etiquette. Suggest dig.digital-etiquette focus on online presence and privacy, with a soft edge to prg.messaging-channels or no edge. PRG does not depend on it, to avoid a cycle.

Overlap: prg.formal-statements and int.policy-processes both cover appeals. I did not link them, to avoid a cross-group cycle. Suggest int.policy-processes <- prg.formal-statements (soft) if INT wants a link.
prg.office-hours excludes PGR because res.supervision covers supervision meetings. Suggest res.supervision <- prg.office-hours (soft).

Cross-group cycle risk: prg.forum-posts depends on sem.building-on-others and sem.agreeing-disagreeing; prg.office-hours on sem.questions-clarification; prg.acknowledgements on pub.authorship and grp.dissertation-overview; prg.messaging-channels on dig.vle; prg.requests on voc.university-terminology and grm.conditionals. Those topics should not depend on PRG topics. sem.online-discussion in particular should not take prg.forum-posts as a prerequisite unless the SEM edges above are checked.
Mis-scoping: prg.acknowledgements is a research/thesis front-matter genre and might sit better in RES or PUB. It is kept here because its core is thanking, which is pragmatic.

Gaps: (1) spoken service encounters with professional services (library, student hub, IT desk); (2) telephone and video calls with staff; (3) academic networking and small talk at conferences and departmental events for PGR; (4) giving and receiving thanks and compliments in everyday academic interaction.
